questions.stem: According to Passage A, an office may submit a case for a series to be retained beyond its scheduled date
options: only during a scheduled review cycle
only if the series records the body's own constitution
at any time, through a review mechanism the documentation describes
only where another office has already made the same request
questions.key: at any time, through a review mechanism the documentation describes
questions.explain: Paragraph 4 states that any office may submit a case for retention beyond the scheduled date, and paragraph 5 confirms the remedy exists. The other three each add a restriction the passage never imposes.

refs.text: any office may submit a case for the retention of a specific series beyond its scheduled date

questions.stem: The narrator in Passage B identifies which of the following as the reason her objection had no effect?
options: the photographs had not been formally accessioned
her supervisor was unwilling to reconsider the schedule
the box had already left the building
the photographs did not fall within the category the series was appraised under
questions.key: the photographs did not fall within the category the series was appraised under
questions.explain: She says the series was appraised as county clerk routine correspondence and photographs are not correspondence, which is why the research-value test could not be reached. That is a scope problem, not unwillingness and not lateness.

refs.text: photographs are not correspondence

questions.stem: The passages differ most sharply in that Passage A
options: recommends a change that Passage B's narrator has already stopped believing in
treats a limitation as a known cost, whereas Passage B treats it as a personal failure
assumes the series is the correct unit of judgment, whereas Passage B shows the unit failing in a specific case
is concerned with the volume of records, whereas Passage B is concerned with their physical condition
questions.key: assumes the series is the correct unit of judgment, whereas Passage B shows the unit failing in a specific case
questions.explain: Passage A justifies series-level appraisal explicitly and locates the remedy in reopening the series, not the item. Passage B is a case where that unit classified the contents out of reach. The volume and condition readings are both false: the box was heavy, not damaged.

refs.text: The series is the unit of judgment

questions.stem: As it is used in Passage A, the word "appraisal" most nearly means
options: an estimate of monetary value
a formal assessment
a criticism of method
an appeal against a decision
questions.key: a formal assessment
questions.explain: The passage defines appraisal as a formal, documented process of examination. The other three shift it to a financial sense or to the review process, which is a separate mechanism the passage distinguishes from appraisal itself.

refs.text: a formal, documented process by which the records of an administrative body are examined

questions.stem: Compared with the narrator of Passage B, the writer of Passage A would most likely describe the review mechanism as
options: adequate
unnecessary
unreliable
discretionary
questions.key: unnecessary
questions.explain: Passage A argues that consistency is obtained by removing judgment from disposal, and presents the criteria as sound; it needs no case-by-case discretion. Passage B's narrator, having seen the mechanism exist unused, is the one positioned to find its adequacy doubtful.

refs.text: Consistency is obtained by removing judgment from the point of disposal.

questions.stem: The tone of the final paragraph of Passage B is best described as
options: resigned
apologetic
outraged
satisfied
questions.key: resigned
questions.explain: She concedes she was probably right, notes the photographs would otherwise have been lost, and ends by conceding the system did what it was built to do. Anger and apology are both available earlier in the passage but neither survives into the last paragraph, and satisfaction is excluded by her not knowing.

refs.text: The system did what it was built to do.

questions.stem: The two passages are similar in that both
options: recommend reform to a records-retention schedule
present a process as sound and describe the cost of that soundness
treat the loss of paperwork as an unavoidable modern condition
argue that individual officers should be permitted to exercise more judgment
questions.key: present a process as sound and describe the cost of that soundness
questions.explain: Passage A calls the apparatus sound and then locates the remedy in reopening the series; Passage B accepts that the system worked and cannot say otherwise. Neither recommends reform, neither argues for more individual discretion, and the paperwork framing belongs to neither.

refs.text: The apparatus is, judged by these criteria, sound.
But that is not the same as the system working.

questions.stem: As it is used in Passage B, the word "wrong" most nearly means
options: incorrect
damaged
in the wrong place
suspicious
questions.key: in the wrong place
questions.explain: She says the box felt wrong, that the boxes should all weigh the same because they should hold the same thing, and that this one was heavy the way a box is heavy when something in it is not what belongs there. The sense is misplacement, not error in judgement or damage.

refs.text: this one was heavy the way a box is heavy when there is something in it that is not paper

questions.stem: The two passages differ in that Passage B's narrator
options: misread the four retention tests
treats an individual box as recoverable where Passage A treats only the series as recoverable
rejects the purpose of retention schedules entirely
believes the photographs were of greater research value than any document in the series
questions.key: treats an individual box as recoverable where Passage A treats only the series as recoverable
questions.explain: That asymmetry is the whole misfit: Passage A puts the remedy in reopening the series, and the narrator's action treats the item as separable. She does not misread the tests, she names the research-value test accurately, and she never questions the schedules' purpose.

refs.text: I said the schedule said the test was research value.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: describe the structure of the human cochlea in detail
argue that an animal's hearing range is shaped by what it must detect
compare the hearing of birds with that of insects
document the decline of ultrasonic hearing in pollinating insects
questions.key: argue that an animal's hearing range is shaped by what it must detect
questions.explain: The moth opens the range argument, the table assembles it, and the wax moth returns to close it. The cochlea is one illustration among several, no birds-and-insects comparison is the point, and no decline is discussed.

refs.text: the ceiling of the audible spectrum is set by ecological circumstance

questions.stem: According to the passage, the four uses to which a barn owl's hearing is put include
options: navigating over long distances and hearing speech
detecting predators and detecting approaching footsteps
echo-ranging insect flight and avoiding parasites
long-distance contact and locating prey by heartbeat
questions.key: echo-ranging insect flight and avoiding parasites
questions.explain: The table gives echo-ranging insect flight to Pipistrellus and avoiding its own ultrasonic parasite to the greater wax moth. Navigation and speech belong to the pigeon and the human, and heartbeat detection is the owl's alone.

refs.text: The barn owl, which hunts in total darkness and locates its prey by rustle

questions.stem: The highest frequency the passage reports for the greater wax moth is
options: 110 kHz
150 kHz
300 kHz
20 kHz
questions.key: 300 kHz
questions.explain: The moth's range is given as high as three hundred kilohertz in the opening paragraph and again in the table. 110 and 150 are the bats and the dolphin, and 20 is the human ceiling.

refs.text: ultrasonic frequencies as high as three hundred kilohertz

questions.stem: As it is used in the passage, the word "inverts" most nearly means
options: reverses
divides
doubles
ignores
questions.key: reverses
questions.explain: The passage contrasts the expectation that a larger animal perceives more with the moth's small body and enormous range, and calls this an inversion of that expectation. The passage also speaks of turning aside in another sense, but here the word names a reversal.

refs.text: it inverts the expectation that an animal's sensory range ought to be a function of its size

questions.stem: According to the table, which two groups are the only ones whose upper limit exceeds that of any bird?
options: the greater wax moth and the domestic dog
the greater wax moth and the bottlenose dolphin
the African elephant and the barn owl
the Pipistrellus bat and the pigeon
questions.key: the greater wax moth and the bottlenose dolphin
questions.explain: The footnote identifies them as the two echolocating entries, which are the greater wax moth at 300 and the dolphin at 150. The dog reaches 45, and every bird in the table is at or below 12, so both named groups are correct and the alternatives are not.

questions.stem: Which detail most directly challenges the traditional account of sensory evolution?
options: the pigeon requires no high frequencies in order to navigate
the owl's cochlea is no better a receptor than a human cochlea
the wax moth's auditory system is small and lightly built, yet it holds the highest upper limit measured
the elephant occupies a band that a human being perceives as pressure rather than sound
questions.key: the wax moth's auditory system is small and lightly built, yet it holds the highest upper limit measured
questions.explain: The traditional account held that more complex structure produced more range, and the passage says it does not survive contact with a moth whose system is small and lightly built and which nonetheless exceeds every vertebrate. The other three are consistent with either account.

refs.text: This account does not survive contact with the wax moth, whose auditory system is small and lightly built

questions.stem: The passage's discussion of a species that is well adapted to a world that then changes is used to show that
options: adaptation is usually the result of competition
an animal's range can become a fixed boundary once its requirements change
evolution operates more rapidly on hearing than on other traits
natural selection cannot be observed in any single species
questions.key: an animal's range can become a fixed boundary once its requirements change
questions.explain: The passage says an owl will not acquire upper frequencies unless its ecosystem changes in a particular way, and that a range which was an advantage becomes a boundary that cannot be crossed from inside. That is a limit argument, not a competition or observation argument.

refs.text: the range that was an advantage becomes a boundary that cannot be crossed from inside.

questions.stem: Which choice most accurately captures the sequence by which the passage says an animal's hearing comes to match its requirements?
options: requirements arise, structure follows, and the range settles at whatever the structure permits
structure varies first, and requirements then adapt to the range available
requirements and structure develop together, with neither leading
range is set by body size, and requirements follow from the range
questions.key: requirements arise, structure follows, and the range settles at whatever the structure permits
questions.explain: The passage says the appropriate solution over a large number of generations was to extend the range until the predator's signal fell inside it, and concludes that the shape of the organ follows the shape of the requirement. Size is explicitly rejected as the driver.

refs.text: the shape of the organ follows the shape of the requirement

questions.stem: The passage's final comparison between the moth and the bat is intended to establish that
options: moths have better hearing than bats
the ceiling of the audible spectrum is not a constant
bats are the only animals that use echo-ranging
comparing two species' hearing is a meaningless exercise
questions.key: the ceiling of the audible spectrum is not a constant
questions.explain: The passage calls hearing better a meaningless question and uses the comparison to show the ceiling is set by circumstance and therefore moves. The third option is contradicted by the footnote's reference to two echolocating entries, and the fourth is stated as a dismissive aside rather than the conclusion.

refs.text: the ceiling of the audible spectrum is set by ecological circumstance and is therefore not a constant. It moves.

questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is to
options: compare the cost of concrete and timber park benches
explain how park furniture came to discourage a particular use
propose a redesign of public seating
argue that landscape architects should consult park users
questions.key: explain how park furniture came to discourage a particular use
questions.explain: The passage traces a design purpose through procurement to installation and declines to call it error. Cost is raised once to rule it out, and both redesign and consultation are explicitly set aside in the closing paragraph.

refs.text: the ordinary operation of a system doing exactly what it was built to do

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following occurred first?
options: the division down the middle of a concrete seat was given a name in the trade
the flat slatted timber bench was displaced by the concrete form
a procurement schedule documented the purpose of a dividing bar
the two designs were placed side by side for comparison
questions.key: the flat slatted timber bench was displaced by the concrete form
questions.explain: The displacement is the event that within two decades made the concrete form the norm, and the naming, the documentation, and the comparison are all described as features of the resulting situation. The passage supplies no earlier date for the timber bench, so the displacement is the earliest datable event among the four.

refs.text: the second has largely displaced the first within two decades

questions.stem: As it is used in the passage, the word "euphemism" most nearly means
options: a pleasant substitute for an unpleasant term
an official classification
a deliberate exaggeration
a term borrowed from another field
questions.key: a pleasant substitute for an unpleasant term
questions.explain: The passage says the features are described functionally and without euphemism, in a context where their purpose is to stop a person lying or sleeping down. The word therefore names a softening of an unpleasant description.

refs.text: described functionally and without euphemism

questions.stem: The passage draws a contrast between the bench as counted in an inventory and the bench as used, on the grounds that
options: inventory counts are usually inaccurate
the count remains accurate while the description of what is counted is not
the two are maintained by different authorities
seat numbers have fallen even where the description holds
questions.key: the count remains accurate while the description of what is counted is not
questions.explain: The passage says the bench is still in the inventory and still counted in assessments of amenity, and that the count is accurate while the description is not, because what was removed was permission. The fall in seat numbers is explicitly denied two paragraphs earlier.

refs.text: the count is accurate while the description is not

questions.stem: The statement that a purpose was "achieved so efficiently that the achievement is now invisible" is used mainly to
options: criticise the contractors who installed the benches
explain why the design is not regarded as a design failure
show that the public rarely uses park furniture
suggest that cheaper designs would work as well
questions.key: explain why the design is not regarded as a design failure
questions.explain: The passage has already ruled out economy, and the closing paragraph says the bench has not failed but has performed. Invisibility to commissioners and unremarkableness to residents are the two parties the passage contrasts, which is what makes it hard to call a failure.

refs.text: the achievement is now invisible to the people who commissioned it and unremarkable to the people who live beside it

questions.stem: Which group does the passage identify as most affected by the loss of usable seating?
options: people for whom a bench is a necessity rather than a convenience
landscape architects
contractors working to a procurement schedule
people who live beside the park
questions.key: people for whom a bench is a necessity rather than a convenience
questions.explain: The passage names a population that is not small and not visible to those who commission benches, requiring a flat surface of a particular width. Architects, contractors, and residents are all named in the passage but as the parties the change is invisible to, not as those affected by it.

refs.text: This matters most to those for whom a bench is not a convenience but a necessity

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that a redesign of public seating
options: is the most useful response to the problem described
would be effective if accompanied by a formal vote
addresses the wrong question, since no design is at fault
should be required before any further installation
questions.key: addresses the wrong question, since no design is at fault
questions.explain: The closing paragraph says the bench has not failed, has performed, and that what we are looking at is not an error in the making of something. It also says nobody is in a position to say no, which locates the problem in authority rather than in the object.

refs.text: We are looking at is not an error in the making of something

questions.stem: The gap beneath the seat of a concrete bench is described as intended to prevent
options: a person from lying down
a person from sleeping
rain from collecting
a person from damaging the surface
questions.key: a person from sleeping
questions.explain: The division prevents lying down and the underseat gap prevents sleeping, in that order. The passage is explicit that the gap exists for the second purpose and not the first.

refs.text: The gap beneath the seat exists to prevent a person from sleeping.

questions.stem: The author's closing claim is best understood as a claim about
options: the expense of municipal procurement
the absence of any point at which a question could have been asked
the failure of landscape architects to understand public needs
the willingness of park users to tolerate inconvenience
questions.key: the absence of any point at which a question could have been asked
questions.explain: Paragraph 3 says the design entered the world through a chain of standards in which nobody asked what the standard was for, and the closing sentence says nobody is in a position to say no. The two together locate the cause in a chain with no decision point, not in cost, incompetence, or public tolerance.

refs.text: at no point in that chain a question being asked about what the standard is for
the difficulty is that this is what the making of things has come to look like when nobody is in a position to say no.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: describe a survey of why patients miss appointments
explain how the narrator's profession is misunderstood
argue that missed appointments reflect a scheduling failure rather than patient forgetfulness
report the financial cost of unused appointment slots
questions.key: argue that missed appointments reflect a scheduling failure rather than patient forgetfulness
questions.explain: The passage rejects the standard explanation in paragraph 3 and supports the scheduling account with survey data and a changed book. The survey is evidence for that claim rather than the subject, and cost appears in the same paragraph as the numbers.

refs.text: Attendance was not the variable. Attendance was the outcome of a set of constraints

questions.stem: According to the passage, the practice turned away how many patients for lack of an available appointment?
options: nine hundred
one thousand and ninety
four thousand two hundred
sixty-one
questions.key: one thousand and ninety
questions.explain: The figure given for patients turned away is one thousand and ninety. Nine hundred is the size of the book, four thousand two hundred is the annual loss of appointments, and sixty-one is the single change's annual recovery.

refs.text: we turned away one thousand and ninety patients for lack of an available appointment

questions.stem: Which of the following does the passage present as evidence against the explanation that patients forget their appointments?
options: the reminders reached some disconnected numbers
the no-show rate is higher for new-patient visits than for follow-ups
most patients reached by telephone said they had known about the appointment
the practice ran at seventy-nine percent of capacity
questions.key: most patients reached by telephone said they had known about the appointment
questions.explain: The survey was made specifically to test the forgetting explanation, and the finding that a clear majority said they had known directly undercuts it. The other three are all consistent with forgetting being real, or bear on capacity rather than on memory.

refs.text: Of two hundred and forty patients who had missed a booked appointment, one hundred and fifty-eight said yes, they knew perfectly well.

questions.stem: Which choice most accurately captures the order in which the practice made its changes?
options: adjusted reminder wording, then shortened the booking window, then moved appointment times
moved appointment times, then allowed cancellation by text, then closed the book earlier
closed the book earlier, then moved appointment times, then altered the reminder system
altered the reminder system, then allowed cancellation by text, then shortened the booking window
questions.key: moved appointment times, then allowed cancellation by text, then closed the book earlier
questions.explain: The changes are given as moving a hundred and forty appointments out of the worst slots, then allowing fortnight's notice by text, then closing the book to new booking at four-thirty. The reminder system is not changed at all, which rules out three of the four.

refs.text: We moved a hundred and forty appointments a year out of eight-thirty and one-fifteen

questions.stem: The narrator's attitude toward her own profession in the final paragraph is best described as
options: defensive
candid
dismissive
ambitious
questions.key: candid
questions.explain: She reports a real improvement, declines to overstate it, admits nine percent is unexplained, and criticises colleagues who claim a single reason. That is candour about the limits of her own evidence, not defensiveness and not ambition.

refs.text: I have a great deal less idea about the rest.

questions.stem: The passage contrasts the practice's operating rate with its rate of turning patients away in order to show that
options: the two figures are calculated differently
a high rate of turning patients away is compatible with unused capacity
capacity should be measured by patient volume rather than slot count
the book should be closed to new booking entirely
questions.key: a high rate of turning patients away is compatible with unused capacity
questions.explain: The passage gives both figures in order to make the point that seventy-nine percent is not full but a book with holes shaped like the hours people cannot attend. Nothing in it suggests a calculation difference or that the book should close.

refs.text: Seventy-nine percent of the book is not full. It is a book with holes shaped like the hours that people cannot attend.

questions.stem: The passage offers the cancellation-by-text figure as support for which claim?
options: late cancellation is never a significant cause of lost slots
a low-cost change can recover appointments at a low cancellation rate
patients prefer text communication to telephone
the eight-thirty slot is always in demand
questions.key: a low-cost change can recover appointments at a low cancellation rate
questions.explain: The fortnight's notice by text is introduced as costing nothing and being cancelled at a rate of under four percent, which is offered as one of several low-cost recoveries. The passage does not say late cancellation is never significant, nor does it compare communication channels.

refs.text: which costs nothing and is cancelled at a rate of under four percent

questions.stem: According to the passage, the most defensible estimate of the share of missed appointments now explained by the narrator's account is
options: a small minority
roughly half
nine tenths
all of them
questions.key: roughly half
questions.explain: She says she knows why a third of them happen and has much less idea about the rest, and the standard explanation is what the survey displaced for just over half the missed patients. Nine tenths is the improvement, not the explained share.

refs.text: I know roughly why a third of them happen

questions.stem: The passage's final remark about colleagues who claim to have solved the problem is best understood as
options: a warning that a single-cause explanation usually rests on poor data
an argument that the residual nine percent cannot be reduced
a defence of the narrator's own survey method
a claim that other practices have worse no-show rates
questions.key: a warning that a single-cause explanation usually rests on poor data
questions.explain: The surest sign she offers of a bad description is having a single reason, which is a general caution rather than a claim about the residual nine percent or about other practices. She has already conceded she cannot generalise her own survey.

refs.text: the surest sign of it is that they have a single reason.
